short_definition: An overdraft happens when you spend more than the available balance in your bank account and the bank covers the shortfall, usually charging fees or interest on the negative balance.
explanation: When a payment exceeds your balance, your bank may pay it and push your account below zero, decline it, or pull money from a linked savings account. This linked option is often called overdraft protection. Some banks offer an arranged overdraft with an agreed limit and interest, while others charge a flat fee for each item they cover. Terms, fees and consumer protections vary widely by country and by bank.

Overdrafts matter because small shortfalls can become expensive. A flat fee on a minor purchase can be far larger than the amount you were short. Repeated or prolonged overdrafts can lead a bank to close your account, and in some countries they can appear on your credit file.

The trade-off is convenience against cost: an overdraft can stop an important payment from bouncing, but it is usually a pricey form of short-term borrowing. Check your bank's fee schedule and your overdraft opt-in or opt-out settings. Turning on low-balance alerts in your banking app is also worthwhile.
example: Illustrative example: You have $40 in checking and buy a $55 meal. If your bank charges a flat $30 overdraft fee (an illustrative figure; check your own bank's fees), covering a $15 shortfall costs you $30. Your balance becomes −$45 until you deposit more money.
common_mistake: Treating an overdraft limit as part of your own money, then staying in the negative for months and paying ongoing fees or interest without noticing.
title: Overdraft
